idiom_name: public static Builder (required params in Builder ctor) + private target constructor; build() throws IllegalStateException
implementation_notes: The Essence role maps one-to-one onto the Effective Java Item 2 builder: the Builder is a public static nested class whose constructor takes every compulsory property (failing fast there with Objects.requireNonNull / IllegalArgumentException), setter-like methods return this for fluent chaining, and build() validates cross-property invariants and throws IllegalStateException naming the missing compulsory properties before the target exists. What replaces the classic structure is constructor restriction plus the builder: the target's constructor is private and nested, so no client outside the class can instantiate an unvalidated instance, and final fields keep compulsory properties immutable after creation (setters exist only on the Builder, never on the target). Essence.validateParameters() becomes an optional validate() on the builder, callable at any time for early feedback. The classic two-class form (separate essence class, package-private target constructor) is still justified when the Essence must live in its own compilation unit, be injected, or create several related target types; a step/staged builder additionally moves 'all compulsory properties supplied' to compile time.
pitfalls: The restricted constructor still leaks inside the class itself: any static factory overload, cached instance, or lazily initialized static field can call the private constructor and skip the Builder's validation - keep exactly one guarded creation path and make every other constructor delegate to it.

The Builder (Essence) is a mutable, non-thread-safe object; sharing one Builder across threads or calling build() concurrently can observe half-supplied properties. Only the built target is thread-safe (immutable), never the Essence.

Frameworks bypass the Essence: Jackson deserializers, JPA/ORM materializers and reflection (setAccessible(true) on the private constructor) create instances without ever calling build(), so invariants checked only in build() do not hold for framework-constructed objects.

Wrong exception type misleads callers: invalid individual setter arguments are IllegalArgumentException, missing compulsory properties at build() are IllegalStateException (Bloch Items 60/72) - conflating the two makes it impossible for clients to distinguish bad input from bad creation sequence.

Checking invariants on Builder fields instead of the target's fields after copying is TOCTOU-vulnerable: the Builder can be mutated while build() copies, so Bloch requires the check on the object fields (Item 39) - do defensive copies for mutable components.

A Builder reused after build() silently produces a second instance from (possibly mutated) state; temporal coupling means the Essence must stay alive and unmodified until createTarget()/build() - document reuse semantics explicitly or make build() idempotent-by-copy.

variants.name: Record with validating compact constructor
variants.idiom_name: record + compact constructor validating all components on every construction path
variants.implementation_notes: Java 16 records collapse the CreationTarget to its compulsory properties (final components, generated accessors, equals/hashCode), and the compact constructor is the validation point: Objects.requireNonNull and range checks run there, and the JLS-guaranteed assignment at the end of the block makes re-assigning a parameter (normalization) effective. Unlike C# this is not 'native': the canonical constructor cannot be hidden (its access must be at least the record's), so the record guarantees always-valid objects on every path but not Essence-restricted creation - any client can call new. Use it when the constructor argument list is short enough to read and framework construction paths (Jackson, JPA) must also validate; add a static factory or a builder whose build() just calls the canonical constructor when readability demands it.
pitfalls: The canonical constructor cannot be made private (JEP 395: its access must be at least as wide as the record's), so presence of all components is guaranteed but the creation path is not - a record alone cannot enforce 'clients must go through the Essence'.

Validation must live in the compact constructor, not in a static factory or builder: those callers can always fall back to new Contract(...) directly, and framework materializers call the canonical constructor directly, skipping any factory-only checks.

Mutable components need defensive copies on the way in (compact constructor) and on the way out (overridden accessor) - record immutability is shallow, so a stored array or List reference keeps the record writable from outside.

variants.name: Immutables generated builder (staged option)
variants.idiom_name: @Value.Immutable generated builder; build() fails on missing mandatory attributes; stagedBuilder makes it a compile error
variants.implementation_notes: The library realization: org.immutables generates the builder from an abstract value type, and the generated build() throws IllegalStateException naming the missing mandatory attributes, with isInitialized()-style early feedback standing in for Essence.validateParameters(). Style(stagedBuilder = true) returns a dedicated intermediate type from each setter so build() only becomes reachable once every mandatory attribute is set, turning the invariant into a compile error - the closest Java gets to C# 11 required members. Choose it when the codebase already runs annotation processors and the number of compulsory properties makes hand-written builders error-prone; the classic form stays preferable when a generated-code dependency is unacceptable.
pitfalls: The runtime failure of build() is a backstop, not a guarantee: missing-attribute errors surface in production at the first call site that builds the object - enable stagedBuilder (compile-time stages) when the mandatory set is part of a public API.
Generated-code mindset trap: attributes without defaults are mandatory by accident of declaration; adding one is a source-compatible but behavior-breaking change for every existing builder call site.
